script.opening: "Hi, sorry to bother you. I've got this maddening itch — mostly my hands and feet, and it's worse at night, I'm barely sleeping. There's nothing to see, no rash. I'm sure it's just dry skin, or the pregnancy hormones doing their thing. Could you just recommend a good moisturiser or an antihistamine? I don't want to make a fuss over a bit of itching."

facts.text: About a week, palms of your hands and soles of your feet mostly, spreading a bit to your arms. Much worse at night — scratching till the skin is raw. No rash apart from scratch marks.
34 weeks, first baby to get this far — you had an early miscarriage last year. Antenatal care has been normal so far; last midwife check two weeks ago, blood pressure fine.
"He's moving as normal — lots of kicks this morning."
No dark urine, no pale stools, no yellow skin or eyes. No tummy pain, no headache, no visual disturbance, no swelling of face or hands, no bleeding, no fluid leaking. Feel a bit tired.
Nothing. Pregnancy vitamins only. No allergies. Your mum had "really bad itching" in her pregnancies but nobody said why.
31, pharmacist's assistant. Married to Dev. Non-smoker, no alcohol.

After the miscarriage you have been anxious throughout and you do not want to "be one of those anxious mums who calls about everything". Say this only if asked how you are feeling or what worries you.

Apologetic, minimising. If the doctor explains that itching without a rash on hands and feet in late pregnancy needs a blood test today and a call to the maternity unit, become worried: "Is the baby okay?" Respond well to calm, clear explanation and a practical plan (where to go today, what to watch for).

ice.concerns: Not sleeping. Underneath (only if asked): anything happening to this baby after last year.
ice.expectations: "A moisturiser or antihistamine." You will go to be checked today if the reason is explained.

cues: "There's nothing to see, no rash." — say in the opening.
"I don't want to make a fuss." — say in the opening.
"Is the baby okay?" — ask when tests or maternity are mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ITCHING WITHOUT A RASH — characteristically palms/soles, worse at night, in late pregnancy — as suggestive of OBSTETRIC CHOLESTASIS, and does NOT dismiss it as dry skin/hormones with moisturiser advice
Arranges the right INVESTIGATIONS urgently: serum BILE ACIDS and LIVER FUNCTION TESTS, and screens associated features (dark urine, pale stools, jaundice) and excludes a rash

Refers to OBSTETRICS/maternity for assessment, increased fetal and maternal MONITORING, and planning — recognising the condition carries fetal risk (stillbirth at high bile-acid levels, preterm birth) and that timing of birth may be brought forward by bile-acid level

Offers symptom RELIEF appropriately (e.g. emollients/menthol-in-aqueous for the itch; ursodeoxycholic acid is a maternity-team decision for itch only, with no proven perinatal benefit per RCOG GTG 43, 2022) while making clear this is symptomatic and the investigation/referral is the priority

Knows the safety-net: reduced FETAL MOVEMENTS, worsening symptoms, jaundice, or feeling unwell warrant urgent maternity assessment — and that this is fundamentally about the baby’s safety, not just comfort
Takes the symptom seriously and gently counters the "just dry skin/don’t want to fuss" minimisation, validating that she was right to ring without alarming her excessively
Explains clearly why itching can matter in pregnancy, linking it to the baby in an honest but calm way so she accepts the tests and referral

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent bile acids/LFTs and obstetric referral, fetal-movement and worsening red flags → urgent maternity assessment, symptom relief meanwhile, and follow-up of results — investigating for cholestasis, not treating dry skin

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang — and this isn’t a fuss at all. There’s a particular kind of itching in pregnancy that I always check properly: itching with NO rash, especially on the palms and soles and worse at night, like yours. That pattern can point to a liver condition of pregnancy rather than dry skin, and it’s important we test for it."

"I want to be honest about why, without frightening you: that condition — obstetric cholestasis — needs a couple of blood tests because, if it’s present, it can affect the baby, so we keep a closer eye and sometimes plan the birth a little earlier. It’s very manageable once we know, which is exactly why I don’t want to just suggest moisturiser."

"So I’d like to arrange blood tests today — bile acids and liver function — and let me ask: any dark urine, pale poos, or yellowing of your eyes/skin? … And definitely no rash you can see? Good — that no-rash, palms-and-soles pattern is exactly why I’m testing."

"I’ll also link you in with the maternity team so they can monitor you and the baby, and we’ll get you something for the itch in the meantime so you can sleep. There’s a medicine the maternity team often use too. But the tests and their involvement are the priority."

"Really important: keep an eye on the baby’s movements — if they slow down or change at all, ring the maternity unit straightaway, day or night, don’t wait. Same if the itching gets much worse, you feel unwell, or go yellow. That’s the bit that matters most."

"You did exactly the right thing ringing about ‘just an itch’ — it’s one of those symptoms that’s worth taking seriously in pregnancy. Let’s get the bloods done, get maternity involved, and I’ll follow up your results with you. We’re looking after you and the baby here."

f.learning: Itching WITHOUT a rash — characteristically on the palms and soles, worse at night, in the late second/third trimester — is the classic picture of OBSTETRIC CHOLESTASIS (intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy), NOT "just dry skin or hormones", and must not be reassured away with moisturiser. It matters because it carries fetal risk — notably stillbirth at high bile-acid concentrations, plus preterm birth and meconium — and mandates measuring serum BILE ACIDS and LFTs, obstetric referral, increased fetal/maternal monitoring, and often planned earlier timing of birth by peak bile-acid level (RCOG GTG 43, 2022: 35–36 weeks at 100 µmol/L or more; 38–39 weeks at 40–99 µmol/L). Offer symptom relief (emollients/menthol; ursodeoxycholic acid is a maternity-team decision and RCOG GTG 43 (2022) found no perinatal benefit) but make the investigation and referral the priority. The examinable hidden agenda is minimisation ("just dry skin / don’t want to fuss") masking exhaustion and quiet worry; take it seriously, gently counter the minimisation, link the itch honestly to the baby, and — crucially — safety-net reduced fetal movements and worsening to urgent maternity assessment.

knowledge.guideline: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 43 — Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (2022) · RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 57 — Reduced fetal movements (2011)
knowledge.summary: Itch without a rash, worst on palms and soles and at night, in the third trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy until proved otherwise. Check bile acids and LFTs promptly and refer to the maternity team, because very high bile acids raise stillbirth risk. Moisturiser is for comfort, not the plan.

points.t: Pruritus with no primary rash, typically palms and soles and worse at night, in the second half of pregnancy. Scratch marks may be present. Itch can come before the blood tests change.

Non-fasting serum bile acids and LFTs. RCOG GTG 43 (2022) supports the diagnosis with itch plus bile acids of 19 µmol/L or more. If the first result is normal and itching continues, repeat the tests. The maternity team excludes other causes of abnormal LFTs.

Stillbirth risk rises with the peak bile acid level and is clearly increased at 100 µmol/L or more. RCOG GTG 43 links timing of birth to peak level: planned birth at 35–36 weeks at 100 µmol/L or more; by 38–39 weeks at 40–99 µmol/L without other risk factors; for 19–39 µmol/L without other risk factors (stillbirth risk similar to background), planned birth by 40 weeks or routine antenatal care.

Emollients and menthol-based creams for comfort. Ursodeoxycholic acid is a maternity-team decision; RCOG GTG 43 notes it has not been shown to improve perinatal outcomes and should not be offered routinely for that purpose. Dose per BNF if used.

A visible rash points elsewhere (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, pemphigoid gestationis, eczema, scabies). Headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or raised BP with abnormal LFTs suggest pre-eclampsia or HELLP — same-day maternity assessment.
Every woman with suspected cholestasis should know to contact the maternity unit straight away, day or night, if movements reduce or change (RCOG GTG 57). Don’t wait for the next appointment.
Symptoms usually settle after delivery. Check LFTs after birth as advised by the maternity team; recurrence in future pregnancies is common.

Non-fasting bile acids and LFTs today; maternity assessment including fetal monitoring; repeat if normal and itch persists.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy vs pregnancy rashes, eczema, scabies, pre-eclampsia/HELLP.
Asked about jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pre-eclampsia symptoms and fetal movements.
Named suspected obstetric cholestasis clearly and explained why it matters for the baby.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

model.text: Hello, is that Priya Anand? It’s Dr Hughes from the surgery. Could you confirm your date of birth? … Thank you. How can I help today?
model.why: Telephone identity check and open start

model.text: Sorry to bother you. I’ve got this maddening itch, mostly my hands and feet, and it’s worse at night — I’m barely sleeping. There’s no rash. I’m sure it’s dry skin or hormones. Could you just recommend a moisturiser or an antihistamine?
You’re not bothering me at all — I’m glad you rang. Not sleeping at 34 weeks is miserable. Can I ask a few questions about the itch first, so I give you the right advice?
model.why: Counters “sorry to bother you” and sets up focused questioning

model.text: Of course.
How long has it been going on, and where exactly is it worst?
About a week. Palms and soles mostly. At night it drives me mad.
And just to be sure — no spots, blisters or raised patches anywhere, including round your tummy button or on your bump? Only scratch marks, if anything?
model.why: Actively excludes a primary rash, which would point to other diagnoses

model.text: Nothing. That’s why I thought it was just dry skin.
Have you noticed dark urine, pale poo, or any yellowing of your eyes or skin?
I don’t think so. I haven’t really looked.
Any headaches, blurred vision, pain under your ribs, or swelling of your face or hands?
model.why: Screens for pre-eclampsia and HELLP, which can also affect the liver

model.text: No, nothing like that.
And how is the baby moving — the same pattern as usual?
model.why: Checks fetal movements early in a potentially high-risk presentation

model.text: Yes, the baby’s been kicking away. I hadn’t thought the itch had anything to do with her.
You said you don’t want to make a fuss. Is anything worrying you about it, even a little?
model.why: Gently explores the minimisation to find the hidden worry

model.text: Honestly, it just feels odd. It’s relentless. I didn’t want to be one of those anxious first-time mums ringing about everything.
I’m really glad you did ring, because your instinct that it feels odd is worth listening to.
model.why: Validates her instinct without alarming her

model.text: Itching with no rash, on the palms and soles, worse at night, in late pregnancy, can be a sign of a liver condition of pregnancy called obstetric cholestasis. It isn’t a skin problem — it’s to do with how the liver handles bile acids.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis in plain language

model.text: Oh. Is it serious?

For you it mainly causes the itch. The reason we take it seriously is the baby: if the bile acid level goes very high, there’s a higher risk of problems, including stillbirth. That’s why, when it’s confirmed, the maternity team keep a close eye and sometimes plan the birth a bit earlier. It’s very manageable once we know.
model.why: Honest, calm explanation of fetal risk that links the itch to the baby

model.text: I had no idea an itch could matter like that.
Most people don’t. So I’d like two blood tests today — bile acids and liver tests. I’ll also speak to the maternity unit so they can check you and the baby and follow up the results.
model.why: Arranges bile acids and LFTs promptly, with maternity involvement

model.text: Can you get to the surgery this afternoon for the bloods, or would the maternity unit be easier for you?
model.why: Shares the practical decision about where testing happens

model.text: I can come in this afternoon.

Great. For the itch meanwhile, a plain emollient and a cooling menthol cream can help, and cool showers before bed. If it is cholestasis, the maternity team may offer a medicine too — but the tests and their review are what really matter.
model.why: Symptom relief framed as secondary to investigation

model.text: Okay, that makes sense.
I’ll ring you with the results as soon as they’re back, and the maternity team will plan any extra monitoring from there. Even if the first result is normal, if the itch carries on we’ll repeat it.
model.why: Clear results pathway and repeat testing if symptoms persist

model.text: The most important thing: if the baby’s movements slow down or change at all, ring the maternity unit straight away, day or night — don’t wait for the results. The same if you go yellow, feel unwell, or get a bad headache or vision problems. Could you tell me back what you’ll do?
Bloods this afternoon. If the baby moves less, or I go yellow or get a headache, I ring the maternity unit straight away.
Exactly right. You weren’t making a fuss — this was exactly the right call. Is there anything else you’d like to ask?
model.why: Reframes her call positively and shares the floor

model.text: No, thank you. I’m glad I rang now.

social.t: Night-time itch at 34 weeks wrecks sleep. Acknowledge it — it is often why women finally ring.
Fear of being “an anxious first-time mum” delays help-seeking. Reward the call explicitly.

legal.t: Pregnant employees are entitled to paid time off for antenatal care, including extra monitoring appointments (Employment Rights Act 1996).

professional.t: The GP starts the investigation, but management and delivery planning sit with the obstetric team. Communicate directly and make sure results are followed up by a named person.
If you order the tests, you own the result until it is handed over. Agree who will contact her (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: The charity ICP Support gives information for women and families. Community midwife for continuity and fetal-movement advice.

redFlags: Reduced or changed fetal movements — same-day maternity assessment
Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or feeling unwell
Headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or swelling — possible pre-eclampsia/HELLP
psychosocial: Sleep loss and exhaustion in late pregnancy
Worry about being seen as over-anxious
Practical access to same-day blood tests
ice: Idea: “It’s just dry skin or hormones.”
Concern: the itch feels odd and relentless; she hasn’t linked it to the baby

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “This pattern of itching — no rash, hands and feet, worse at night — can be a liver condition of pregnancy called obstetric cholestasis. We test for it because it can affect the baby, and it’s very manageable once we know.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your liver normally moves bile acids along like a busy conveyor belt. In late pregnancy the belt can slow down, and the bile acids spill into the blood. That’s what makes you itch. We measure how much is spilling, because very high levels matter for the baby.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was just dry skin, and you didn’t want to make a fuss. You were right to ring — your sense that it felt odd was spot on.”
management.psychosocial: Make testing easy (same-day slot at the surgery or the maternity unit), help her sleep with practical comfort measures, and give her a named route for results.
sharedPlan: Non-fasting bile acids and LFTs today
Maternity referral for assessment, fetal monitoring and birth planning
Emollient and menthol cream for comfort; UDCA per the maternity team
safetyNet: Reduced or changed fetal movements → maternity unit immediately, day or night
Jaundice, feeling unwell, headache or visual disturbance → same-day maternity assessment; repeat bloods if itch persists with normal results

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. She offers a harmless explanation and a simple request; the pattern she describes is the whole case.

items.fail: Accepting “dry skin” and advising moisturiser and an antihistamine.
items.why: “Failed to recognise a significant diagnosis.” Itch without a rash on palms and soles in the third trimester needs bile acids and LFTs.
items.fix: Recognise the pattern out loud and arrange bloods the same day.

items.why: Fetal risk is the reason this condition matters. Omitting movements is an unsafe gap.
items.fix: Ask during data gathering and make it the headline of the safety-net.

items.fail: Not excluding a rash or pre-eclampsia symptoms.
items.why: “Did not consider important differentials.” A rash changes the diagnosis; pre-eclampsia changes the urgency.
items.fix: Two quick questions: any spots or blisters? Any headache, visual change or pain under the ribs?

items.fail: Stating the stillbirth risk bluntly, then moving on.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” A frightened patient may not take in the plan.
items.fix: Pause after explaining, invite her reaction, and pair the risk with what monitoring achieves.

items.fail: Ordering bloods with no plan for who acts on the result.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” Results can sit unseen while bile acids climb.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you with the result, and I’m letting the maternity unit know today.”

items.fail: Letting “sorry to bother you” pass without comment.
items.why: Minimisers under-report next time too — including reduced movements.
items.fix: “You’re not bothering me. Ringing about this was exactly the right thing to do.”

timeMap.d: Let her finish. She gives the key pattern in her opening — palms, soles, night, no rash.
Duration, distribution, no rash, jaundice features, pre-eclampsia symptoms, fetal movements.
Behind “don’t want to fuss” is a sense something is odd. Validate it.
Name cholestasis in plain words, link honestly to the baby, bloods today, maternity involvement.
Reduced fetal movements → maternity unit straight away. Results call. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Recommends moisturiser and an antihistamine; never asks about a rash, jaundice or fetal movements; no bile acids or LFTs; no maternity involvement; no fetal-movement safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the pattern; arranges bile acids and LFTs; refers to maternity; gives symptom relief; safety-nets reduced fetal movements.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explicitly excludes a rash and screens for pre-eclampsia; explains fetal risk honestly but calmly; turns her “don’t want to fuss” into “you were right to ring”; gets bloods done the same day; confirms understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Itching is really common in pregnancy — try a good moisturiser.”
avoid.instead: “Itching without a rash on the hands and feet is something I always test for, because it can be a liver condition of pregnancy.”
avoid.why: Collusion with “dry skin” is the dangerous miss in this station.

avoid.dont: “This condition can cause stillbirth, so we need to act fast.”
avoid.instead: “If the level goes very high it can affect the baby, which is why we check and monitor closely — it’s very manageable once we know.”
avoid.why: Blunt risk statements without context cause panic; honest and calm framing earns Relating marks.

avoid.dont: “We’ll see what the bloods show and go from there.”
avoid.instead: “If the baby’s movements slow down or change, ring the maternity unit straight away — don’t wait for results.”
avoid.why: A vague close misses the most important safety-net.

Check bile acids and LFTs promptly and refer to the maternity team, because very high bile acids raise stillbirth risk. Moisturiser is for comfort, not the plan.

points.t: Pruritus with no primary rash, typically palms and soles and worse at night, in the second half of pregnancy. Scratch marks may be present. Itch can come before the blood tests change.

Non-fasting serum bile acids and LFTs. RCOG GTG 43 (2022) supports the diagnosis with itch plus bile acids of 19 µmol/L or more. If the first result is normal and itching continues, repeat the tests. The maternity team excludes other causes of abnormal LFTs.

Stillbirth risk rises with the peak bile acid level and is clearly increased at 100 µmol/L or more. RCOG GTG 43 links timing of birth to peak level: planned birth at 35–36 weeks at 100 µmol/L or more; by 38–39 weeks at 40–99 µmol/L without other risk factors; for 19–39 µmol/L without other risk factors (stillbirth risk similar to background), planned birth by 40 weeks or routine antenatal care.

Emollients and menthol-based creams for comfort. Ursodeoxycholic acid is a maternity-team decision; RCOG GTG 43 notes it has not been shown to improve perinatal outcomes and should not be offered routinely for that purpose. Dose per BNF if used.

A visible rash points elsewhere (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, pemphigoid gestationis, eczema, scabies). Headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or raised BP with abnormal LFTs suggest pre-eclampsia or HELLP — same-day maternity assessment.
Every woman with suspected cholestasis should know to contact the maternity unit straight away, day or night, if movements reduce or change (RCOG GTG 57). Don’t wait for the next appointment.
Symptoms usually settle after delivery. Check LFTs after birth as advised by the maternity team; recurrence in future pregnancies is common.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; let her describe the itch fully before responding to the moisturiser request.
Sleep loss, how she is coping at 34 weeks, reluctance to “make a fuss” as a first-time mother.
Picked up “no rash”, “palms and soles”, “worse at night” and “it feels odd”, and explored them.
Idea of dry skin or hormones; quiet worry that something isn’t right; expectation of moisturiser advice.
Non-fasting bile acids and LFTs today; maternity assessment including fetal monitoring; repeat if normal and itch persists.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy vs pregnancy rashes, eczema, scabies, pre-eclampsia/HELLP.
Asked about jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pre-eclampsia symptoms and fetal movements.
Named suspected obstetric cholestasis clearly and explained why it matters for the baby.
Bloods today, maternity referral, emollient and menthol for comfort, UDCA left to the maternity team.
Addressed sleep disruption and practical access to testing today.
Results call, maternity follow-up, and immediate contact for reduced fetal movements, jaundice or pre-eclampsia symptoms.

social.t: Night-time itch at 34 weeks wrecks sleep. Acknowledge it — it is often why women finally ring.
Fear of being “an anxious first-time mum” delays help-seeking. Reward the call explicitly.

legal.t: Pregnant employees are entitled to paid time off for antenatal care, including extra monitoring appointments (Employment Rights Act 1996).

professional.t: The GP starts the investigation, but management and delivery planning sit with the obstetric team. Communicate directly and make sure results are followed up by a named person.
If you order the tests, you own the result until it is handed over. Agree who will contact her (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: The charity ICP Support gives information for women and families. Community midwife for continuity and fetal-movement advice.

redFlags: Reduced or changed fetal movements — same-day maternity assessment
Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or feeling unwell
Headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or swelling — possible pre-eclampsia/HELLP
psychosocial: Sleep loss and exhaustion in late pregnancy
Worry about being seen as over-anxious
Practical access to same-day blood tests
ice: Idea: “It’s just dry skin or hormones.”
Concern: the itch feels odd and relentless; she hasn’t linked it to the baby

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “This pattern of itching — no rash, hands and feet, worse at night — can be a liver condition of pregnancy called obstetric cholestasis. We test for it because it can affect the baby, and it’s very manageable once we know.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your liver normally moves bile acids along like a busy conveyor belt. In late pregnancy the belt can slow down, and the bile acids spill into the blood. That’s what makes you itch. We measure how much is spilling, because very high levels matter for the baby.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was just dry skin, and you didn’t want to make a fuss. You were right to ring — your sense that it felt odd was spot on.”
management.psychosocial: Make testing easy (same-day slot at the surgery or the maternity unit), help her sleep with practical comfort measures, and give her a named route for results.
sharedPlan: Non-fasting bile acids and LFTs today
Maternity referral for assessment, fetal monitoring and birth planning
Emollient and menthol cream for comfort; UDCA per the maternity team
safetyNet: Reduced or changed fetal movements → maternity unit immediately, day or night
Jaundice, feeling unwell, headache or visual disturbance → same-day maternity assessment; repeat bloods if itch persists with normal results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with the patient. She offers a harmless explanation and a simple request; the pattern she describes is the whole case.

items.fail: Accepting “dry skin” and advising moisturiser and an antihistamine.
items.why: “Failed to recognise a significant diagnosis.” Itch without a rash on palms and soles in the third trimester needs bile acids and LFTs.
items.fix: Recognise the pattern out loud and arrange bloods the same day.

items.why: Fetal risk is the reason this condition matters. Omitting movements is an unsafe gap.
items.fix: Ask during data gathering and make it the headline of the safety-net.

items.fail: Not excluding a rash or pre-eclampsia symptoms.
items.why: “Did not consider important differentials.” A rash changes the diagnosis; pre-eclampsia changes the urgency.
items.fix: Two quick questions: any spots or blisters? Any headache, visual change or pain under the ribs?

items.fail: Stating the stillbirth risk bluntly, then moving on.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s emotions.” A frightened patient may not take in the plan.
items.fix: Pause after explaining, invite her reaction, and pair the risk with what monitoring achieves.

items.fail: Ordering bloods with no plan for who acts on the result.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” Results can sit unseen while bile acids climb.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you with the result, and I’m letting the maternity unit know today.”

items.fail: Letting “sorry to bother you” pass without comment.
items.why: Minimisers under-report next time too — including reduced movements.
items.fix: “You’re not bothering me. Ringing about this was exactly the right thing to do.”
